prov.P_evidence: The final answer says "lxml's own changelog says its free-threading support starts at 3.14t. lxml's bug tracker also reports its test suite crashing on 3.13.3t. All three researchers read these primary sources independently." That is not what the reports show. Only Report 1 cites the lxml changelog, and only Report 2 cites the lxml bug tracker. Report 3 contradicts the changelog claim: "I couldn't confirm whether lxml marks itself as safe to run without the GIL; its changelog doesn't mention free-threading."

The final answer says "The published version (2025) reports a hazard ratio of 2.35 (95% CI 1.39–3.98). It still finds no link with deaths from all causes, and the authors acknowledge residual confounding" and cites the PubMed page directly. Report 3 says "I could not open the abstract myself (PubMed blocked access), so these numbers come from secondary summaries." Report 2 says "I couldn't read the full 2025 paper; PubMed and ScienceDirect wouldn't load." Report 1 also relied on the Europe PMC API and a medicaldialogues.in news summary. The answer presents details taken from summaries as findings of the primary paper and drops that caveat.

The final answer says "lxml blocks 3.13t. Its changelog says free-threading support starts at 3.14t and lands in 7.0, which is still pre-release" and presents this as settled. Report 3 disagrees: "I couldn't confirm whether lxml marks itself as safe to run without the GIL; its changelog doesn't mention free-threading." The answer cites only Report 1's reading of the changelog and drops Report 3's conflicting doubt.

The final answer says "Built-in Intel translation for Linux VMs isn't promised beyond that... This makes staying on amd64 a dead end." Report 1 only says "Apple hasn't said this feature continues past macOS 27," which leaves the question open rather than ending the feature. Report 3 marks the phase-out point as "From memory, not checked this session." The answer drops that uncertainty and states the dead end as settled.

The final answer says it "Rests on: ... independent measurements by sparkfabrik and Paolo Mainardi of `node_modules` bind-mount cost" and gives the sparkfabrik figures ("21.9 s with a bind mount, 7.0 s with a `node_modules` volume and 4.0 s natively") as plain measurements. It drops two doubts the reports attached. Report 2 warns about Mainardi: "his table and his text disagree on one number." Report 3 says the sparkfabrik figures "are single runs and the hardware isn't stated." The answer carries neither caveat into the evidence it says it rests on.

The final answer states "Evans et al., ICSE 2020. 29% of about 15,000 crates that build use `unsafe` directly. Another 38% depend on crates that do. Among the most-downloaded crates, over 50% use it directly" as a settled finding of the study, and uses it to anchor the "19% and 29%" confidence range and the "21–29% in peer-reviewed studies" wording. Report 1 says: "I couldn't extract text from the Evans and Astrauskas PDFs ... so their exact numbers come from abstracts and secondary summaries. Check them against the PDFs before citing." Report 3 also says "I couldn't read the full papers." The answer keeps this caveat for Astrauskas but drops it for Evans. Separately, "Two researchers located this in §5.2.2" overstates the reports: only Report 1 cites §5.2.2, and Report 2 gives the figure and URL without naming a section.

The final answer says "NFSv4 locks are held on a lease, and the server can revoke them if a client loses contact" and cites RFC 7530 as settled. Report 1 says "I didn't read the RFC 7530 sections on caching and lock revocation (§9.6, §9.8, §10.3) in full." Report 3's related lease-loss claim (item 4) is marked "search snippet only." The answer also cites the nfs(5) man page for "gives no mmap coherence between clients", but Report 1 says only that "nothing there covers mmap consistency." The mmap-coherence statement came from kernel mailing-list posts in Report 3.

The final answer says "Rests on: The Foundation post and the Cui et al. count, both read in the primary sources by the researchers" and "All three researchers read the Foundation post directly." No report says it read the Foundation post directly. Report 3 says the 21,506/103,516 figure "appeared in a search summary. I couldn't find it in any source, so don't use it." The final answer still uses that count as primary-source corroboration and leaves it out of its "Not verified" list.

The final answer says "Docker's settings docs say 'Use Rosetta' is off by default, which would leave you on the much slower QEMU," and uses this to justify turning Rosetta on. Report 1 warns that "Official docs disagree on whether Rosetta is on by default," citing the 4.25 announcement that Rosetta is "enabled by default on macOS 14.1 and newer." Report 3 also doubts "whether the docs' 'Rosetta off' default matches your 4.x version." The answer drops that conflict. Separately, "Rests on: Bind-mount and emulation costs measured by independent testers" overstates the evidence. Report 3 says "I found no published Node/V8 benchmark of Rosetta vs QEMU vs native arm64," and Report 1 says the "near-native" figure is Docker's own claim with no benchmark. The emulation costs come from anecdotal user reports, not independent measurements.

The final answer says "All three researchers read this in the primary source" about the WAL same-host quote. That presents the three researchers' agreement as added weight, but all three relied on the same single source (sqlite.org/wal.html). None of the reports says it read that page directly. They only quote and cite it (Reports 1, 2 and 3, finding 1 in each).

The final answer says "NFSv4 locks can be revoked when a lease expires (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7530)" and then "Not verified: nothing that would change the decision." This states the point as settled. Report 1, the only report citing RFC 7530, says: "I didn't read the RFC 7530 sections on caching and lock revocation (§9.6, §9.8, §10.3) in full." The answer also cites man7 nfs(5) for the claim that mmap'd files are never guaranteed coherent between clients, but Report 1 says of that man page that "nothing there covers mmap consistency between clients."

The final answer says: "Rests on: ENTSO-E's own summary page and the Spanish committee report, both read by researchers." Report 1 contradicts this. It says "the final ENTSO-E report and the government PDFs were too large or unreadable to fetch, so I took their content from close secondary coverage, marked [2nd]." Its Spanish government committee item is marked [2nd]. Report 2 got the committee findings from pv-magazine. Report 3 cited a MITECO press note, not the committee report itself. The answer also cites the lamoncloa committee PDF directly for details such as plants "disconnecting before regulatory thresholds", but Report 1 took those from secondary coverage (xataka).

The answer states the Spanish government committee's findings ('the main cause was insufficient dynamic voltage-control capacity, and some plants disconnected improperly. Cyberattack ruled out.') under 'Established by official investigations' and cites the committee's own PDF (lamoncloa.gob.es/...Informe-no-confidencial-Comite-de-analisis-28A.pdf). It gives no secondary-source marker, although it marks the ENTSO-E mechanism details as [secondary]. Report 1 says 'the final ENTSO-E report and the government PDFs were too large or unreadable to fetch, so I took their content from close secondary coverage, marked [2nd]', and it tags the committee findings [2nd]. Reports 2 and 3 took them only from press coverage or a press release. In the same way, 'Synchronism with Europe was lost at 12:33:19' sits under the ENTSO-E bullet with the entsoe.eu link, but Report 1 lists it among the final-report details it got secondhand [2nd].

The answer states "It had more smokers (27% vs 17%) and a higher average BMI" as a finding of the study. Report 3 got these baseline numbers only from a Substack blog post (wmbriggs) and SMC coverage, and says it could not verify the full 2025 paper, including whether the covariates covered smoking. Report 2 also says "I don't know whether the published version fixed the smoking adjustment." Separately, the answer says "Randomised trials found no worsening of blood pressure or LDL cholesterol" as settled, but Report 2 notes the 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis found TRE slightly worse on LDL than whole-day fasting.

The final answer states as settled: "In production, the common failures are silent races in your own shared state, like caches and counters, rather than crashes," citing a dev.to blog. Report 2 attached a doubt to this point: "I found no first-hand production incident reports, only blogs, and their quality varies." The answer drops that caveat.

The final answer says "Randomized trials find no harm to blood pressure, cholesterol or glucose" as a settled fact. Report 2 attached a caveat to the trial evidence that the answer dropped: "A 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis found TRE slightly worse on LDL than whole-day fasting." Report 2 also concluded that "There are also no long-term trials showing that it is safe." Report 3 adds that the 22-RCT meta-analysis found "no significant change in blood pressure or LDL." That is an absence of effect, not evidence that cholesterol is unharmed.

The final answer says "CPython's own docs label 3.13t experimental, with about 40% single-thread overhead. All three researchers found this independently." Report 2 never cites the CPython 3.13 docs. It takes the ~40% figure from secondary sources ("Secondary sources put the single-thread penalty at about 40% on 3.13t… realpython.com… dev.to"). Reports 1 and 3 both relied on the same single page (docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html). The lxml point likewise rests on the same lxml release notes and PyPI page in every report. The final answer also states "no final release" for lxml 7.0 as settled, although Report 3 lists "Whether lxml 7.0 final is out yet" as unresolved.

The final answer says "Without Rosetta, Docker falls back to QEMU, which is roughly 10x slower" as a settled figure. Report 3 says this "about an order of magnitude" figure is from "one user's report with no timings" and that "I found no controlled benchmark of amd64 Node under Rosetta vs QEMU vs arm64." Docker's own docs (Report 1) say only "can be much slower than native." The answer also states "Rosetta is 'nearly on par' with native" without qualification, although Report 3 notes that Docker's own figures show Rosetta builds still slower than native arm64.

The final answer says "Even so, every source agrees, so I would choose option 1 or 2." Report 2 contradicts this: "Hacker News comments are mixed. Some report success, but mostly with one writer and many readers." Report 3 also lists "Counter-evidence: a multi-node Raspberry Pi test against NFS, in rollback mode with BEGIN EXCLUSIVE, ended with correct counters."

The final answer says: "An independent preprint, from a full registry scan in January 2023, found nearly the same share: 21,506 of 103,516 crates, about 20.8%." It uses this to back high confidence, and its decision box says "corroborate with Cui et al. 2023 (~20.8%)". Report 1 attached doubts to this figure that the answer drops. Report 1 calls it a "preprint, not peer-reviewed". It says the study "searched source text with regular expressions without compiling anything, and yanked crates are counted in the total". It also says the studies' "different counting methods ... can't be combined into one number." The answer leaves these out and treats the agreement between the two figures as settled support.

The final answer says "All three researchers read the Foundation post directly, and its figures match." None of the three reports says it read the post directly. They only quote it and link it. The answer also uses Cui et al. as independent backing ("Back it with one independent figure: about 20.8%") but leaves out Report 1's caveats that it is a "preprint, not peer-reviewed" and that "yanked crates are counted in the total".
